drainage.local_h: Why sand over clay holds water in Big Sandy
local: Big Sandy sits on deep sand, and that surprises people who see a pond in the backyard. The sand takes water in fast. Then it reaches the clay layer underneath, stops, and spreads out. High ground clears in hours, but the low corner near the creek or a ditch can stay wet for days, because that is where the water collects and has nowhere to go. Neither is a mystery once we trace where the water travels.

Many drainage calls out here come down to two spots. One is the bottom of the lot. The other is the side of the house where a downspout dumps into flat sand over clay. Before anyone digs a trench, we trace the flow, ideally during or right after a rain. Half the yards we are called to for a French drain turn out not to need one, and a regrade or a solid-pipe downspout reroute does the job. A rain is the best time to look, so we like to walk the lot then when we can.

When water is trapped in the ground, a French drain is the right tool. We use sock-wrapped 4-inch perforated pipe over #57 stone, backfilled with stone, and tie it to a daylighted outlet or a pop-up emitter. On larger lots there is usually somewhere lower on the property to send the water, which helps. A buried dead end just backs up and fails. Surface grading, catch basins and a dry creek bed or sod on top finish the job.

Price follows the work. Small fixes like a downspout reroute or one low spot run $450 to $1,000, a standard single run is $1,900 to $3,000, full systems run $3,000 to $4,500 and large combined projects start at $4,500. Most land at $2,000 to $3,750. Pipe length, dig depth, the outlet and the finish on top set the number. You get all of it in a written, itemized estimate that says what we are installing and why.

faq.q: Can you fix water standing near my house in Big Sandy?
faq.a: Usually, yes. We find where the water comes from, then regrade the soil away from the slab, reroute downspouts or run a French drain to a daylighted outlet. Small fixes run about $450 to $1,000, and most full projects run $2,000 to $3,750.

faq.q: Part of my yard stays wet for days after rain. Is that normal here?
faq.a: It is common in the low spots around Big Sandy, where sand sits on a clay layer. Water drains through the sand, hits the clay and spreads out. A regrade, swale or French drain usually fixes it. We look at where the water goes before recommending anything.

faq.q: Do I really need a French drain?
faq.a: Maybe not. Many soggy yards are fed by surface water: roof runoff, a driveway sloping back toward the house or a neighbor's higher lot. Those are fixed with downspout reroutes and regrading, for less money. A French drain is for water already in the ground, like a spot that stays spongy for days.

faq.q: What does a French drain cost?

faq.q: When is the best time to have drainage fixed?
faq.a: We work year-round, but the best time to see the problem is during or right after a rain. Digging goes faster in a dry stretch. Getting it done before the spring rains means you do not spend another season with a pond in the back corner.

fertilization.local_h: A feeding plan for sand over clay
local: Sand is the first thing to know about feeding a Big Sandy lawn. It takes water fast and gives it up fast, and fertilizer travels with the water. A quick-release product on deep sand can wash below the roots after the first hard rain. That is why we use slow-release product timed to the week the grass can use it, and why we pull a soil sample before we plan anything.

You rarely need to feed every acre. On a big lot we aim the program at the lawn around the house and out front, where it shows and gets used, and leave the outer ground alone. That keeps the cost in check and puts the product where you will see it. Tell us how much of the lot you consider the yard, and the written plan will be built on that area.

The schedule follows the soil, not the store shelf. The first feeding goes down around April 25, once nights hold above 60 degrees. A lighter, summer-safe feeding in early July keeps the lawn from running on empty when August turns dry and sand lawns start to burn. The last real nitrogen goes down in early September, and October is potassium only. Skipping March matters on sand, since an early feeding washes through before the grass can use it.

Pines drop acidic needles year after year, and many East Texas soils test a little low on pH, so we add lime when the test calls for it. Down near Big Sandy Creek, clay under the sand packs hard, and those low pockets are where core aeration pays off. Late August to mid-September is the window, with the feeding right behind it. We coordinate the visits with your mowing schedule so the product goes down the week the grass can use it.

faq.q: How much does lawn fertilization cost in Big Sandy?
faq.a: Visits start from about $190. A full program is usually four visits, and the price depends on how much lawn we are feeding, the grass type, whether the soil test calls for lime and whether you add aeration. We give you the plan and the price in writing before the first application.

faq.q: Is it worth fertilizing a whole acre?
faq.a: Usually not. We focus feedings on the lawn you see and use, around the house and out front, and leave the outer ground alone. That keeps the cost down and puts the product where it counts. If you do want more of the lot fed, we measure it and price it the same way.

faq.q: When is the first feeding of the year?
faq.a: Around April 25, once overnight lows hold above 60 degrees and the grass is fully awake. Feeding in March mostly washes out with the next rain, and on sandy ground it washes out faster, because Bermuda and St. Augustine are still half-dormant and cannot pull it in.

faq.q: Do you aerate lawns around Big Sandy?
faq.a: Yes, with a core aerator that pulls plugs instead of poking holes. The sandy high ground usually needs it less. The clay pockets near the creek are where compaction shows up. We aerate between late August and mid-September, and the lawn should be watered the day before so the tines bite.

faq.q: Do Bermuda and St. Augustine need a winterizer?
faq.a: Not the high-nitrogen kind sold for northern lawns. Late nitrogen pushes soft growth the frost burns off, and on St. Augustine it can feed large patch. Our October feeding is low in nitrogen and heavy in potassium, which helps rooting and cold hardiness, when the soil test says the lawn needs it.

flower-bed-installation.local_h: Beds that handle full sun on an open lot
local: Beds on open Big Sandy lots take full afternoon sun with nothing to break it. That rules out a lot of what garden centers stock in April. We reach for lantana, salvia, plumbago and annual vinca, which hold their color through July and August. Vinca waits until the soil is truly warm, usually mid-May, because a cool, wet spring rots it. Petunias and impatiens look great in April and are crispy sticks by the Fourth of July.

Then there is the sand. It drains fast, so a bed dug straight into it dries out between rains. Compost goes in first, worked through the top of the soil, so the bed holds water longer and the roots have something to grab. We also pull every weed by the root and loosen the top of the soil before a single plant goes in. Mulch goes on last, pulled back off the stems, at 1 to 1.5 inches.

Layout matters on a big lot, where a small bed gets lost. We shape a bed to read from the road and from the porch, with perennials and shrubs as the backbone and seasonal color on top. Where a spot near the creek or a low corner stays wet, we adjust the bed or the grade first rather than plant into standing water. Plants go in with real spacing so air moves through them.

Fall is the best window for shrubs and perennials, September through November, while the soil is warm. Spring planting works too, but new beds need more water through their first summer. If you want to see the bed before we dig, the $199 Flower Bed Preview gives you a rendering and plant list, credited toward an install booked within 90 days. Before we leave, we walk you through watering so the new plants make it through their first summer.

faq.q: How much does a new flower bed cost in Big Sandy?
faq.a: New beds are priced with our landscaping and planting work, where most projects run $900 to $3,600. A small refresh of an existing bed starts at a few hundred dollars. Bed size, plant count and size, edging material and how much soil prep is needed set the price.

faq.q: What flowers hold up in full afternoon sun?
faq.a: Lantana, annual vinca, salvia and plumbago hold their color through July and August in full sun, along with knockout roses. All of them want good drainage and hate being overwatered. Lantana and plumbago are often root-hardy here and come back in spring.

faq.q: When is the best time to plant flower beds here?
faq.a: Shrubs and perennials do best planted in fall, when the soil is still warm and roots keep growing through winter. Heat lovers like vinca wait until the soil warms up in mid-May. Spring planting works too, but new beds need more water through their first summer.

faq.q: Why do you add compost to sandy ground?
faq.a: Sand drains fast, so plants dry out between rains. Compost worked into the top of the soil helps the bed hold water and gives roots more to work with. We do it on every bed before planting, and we mulch on top at 1 to 1.5 inches to slow evaporation.

faq.q: Can I see a design before you plant?

hardscaping.local_h: Building on sand without it shifting
local: On the bigger lots around Big Sandy, the usual request is a patio off the back porch with a fire pit a few steps out into the yard. There is room for both, so the question is how to build them to last. Most of the answer is under the surface, in a ground that is deep sand in places and clay in the low spots. The sand drains well, but it does not hold a shape, so most of the work is in the base.

Loose sand will creep sideways and let the edges of a patio drift apart. So we dig out to the right depth, lay and compact a crushed stone base, and lock the edges with a border so nothing can move out from under the field. Chopped stone borders do that job and look finished. The patio is pitched away from the house so roof water goes out into the yard.

Low pockets near the creek or a ditch are the other thing we look for. Sand sits on clay there, and water gets trapped. If the patio will sit low, catch roof runoff or lie at the bottom of a slope, we plan the drainage first, because water getting under a patio is what undermines it. Sometimes that means a small swale or a regrade before the first stone. We would rather spend a day on grade than have you rebuild a sunken corner later.

Pavers, flagstone and chopped stone are all on the table. Most projects run $3,100 to $9,100, set by square footage, the material, the base work and how easily we can get equipment and stone to the spot. If you want to see it first, the $449 Hardscape Preview gives layout renderings and is credited toward a build booked within 90 days. The estimate is written and itemized, so you see the base work as its own line.

faq.q: How much does a patio and fire pit cost in Big Sandy?

faq.q: How do you keep a patio from shifting in sandy ground?
faq.a: By building the base right. We dig out to the proper depth, compact a crushed stone base, lock the edges with a border so loose sand cannot creep and pitch the surface away from the house. Where the spot is low or wet, drainage gets planned before we set the first piece.

hedge-trimming.local_h: Two kinds of hedge on a Big Sandy property
local: Big Sandy properties tend to have two different hedge jobs. One is the foundation shrubs along the house, a handful of plants you pass every day. The other is a screen: a long row of hollies or ligustrum along a property line, a drive or a road. They need different handling and they price differently, so we count and measure each before we quote. The foundation job is usually quick, and the screen is where the hours and the price are.

Foundation shrubs get shaped a little wider at the base than at the top, so light reaches the lower branches and they do not go bare underneath. Hollies and ligustrum want early summer, after the spring flush hardens off. Azaleas get cut within a few weeks of finishing bloom, or you clip off next year's flowers. We note which is which on the walkthrough. A hedge shaped narrower at the bottom than the top goes bare and leggy underneath.

Screens are about length and height. On a lot with acreage, a row can run a long way, and the price follows the footage and how tall you want it kept. We bring big screens down to a height you can live with and hold it there. A hedge that has been left for years may need a hard cut, and it can look rough for a season while it fills back in.

Out here the clippings add up, so haul-off is priced into the quote. Tarps go down before we start, and we rake, blow the beds clean and take it all with us. Skip hard shearing in late fall, because the tender regrowth burns brown in the first cold snap. Most hedges want two to three trims between spring and fall, and we can set a recurring schedule. Debris volume and access around the beds are part of the price.

faq.q: How much does hedge trimming cost in Big Sandy?
faq.a: Most jobs run $150 to $800. A few foundation shrubs sit at the low end, while long rows, tall hedges and shrubs that have not been touched in years run higher. Hauling off the clippings is part of the job. We walk the property and send a written, itemized quote, usually within a day.

faq.q: How often should a privacy hedge be trimmed?
faq.a: Once a year is the minimum for most hollies, ligustrum and wax myrtles, in early summer after the spring flush. Fast growers may need a second, lighter trim in early fall. Waiting several years means a hard cut that leaves the hedge thin for a season, so a steady schedule is easier on the plant.

faq.q: Can you bring back a hedge that has gotten away from me?
faq.a: Usually, yes. We do hard rejuvenation cuts on overgrown shrubs and take them back to a size they can grow into. It can look rough while it fills in. Some plants handle it better than others, so we tell you on the walkthrough whether yours will come back or should be replaced.

faq.q: When is the right time to trim hollies, boxwoods and azaleas?
faq.a: Hollies and boxwoods get shaped in early June, once the spring flush has hardened off. Azaleas and mophead hydrangeas get cut right after they bloom, because they set next year's buds on this year's stems. If you keep a holly for winter berries, we cut lighter so some of the berries survive.

faq.q: Do you haul away the trimmings?
faq.a: Yes. Tarps go down before we start, and every clipping is raked up, blown out of the beds and hauled off when we finish. You will not be left with a brush pile. Debris volume is part of the quote, so a big rejuvenation job is priced with the haul-off already in it.

irrigation.local_h: Watering sand that drinks fast and dries fast
local: Big Sandy earns its name in a dry August. Deep sand takes water quickly and lets it go just as quickly, so a lawn here can look fine on Monday and stressed by Friday. A sprinkler system helps, but only if it is laid out for how the yard behaves. We walk the lot first and note the sun, the shade, the slope and where the water source is. Spring and fall are the best times to put a new system in.

We do not try to irrigate acreage that does fine on rain. We water the part of the property you actually use, which is the lawn around the house and the beds, and we zone it by sun and shade. Open turf in full afternoon sun gets its own zone, and the shaded St. Augustine near the tree line gets another. Shorter cycles let water soak in before it runs through.

Beds go on drip instead of spray heads. Spray in a bed wets the leaves, the mulch and the house and still leaves the roots thirsty, while drip puts the water at the roots and keeps foliage dry. Out on country lots, water source and pressure can vary from place to place, so we check both before we design anything. On city water, a backflow device is part of the install.

Texas treats irrigation as licensed work, and ours is done under a licensed irrigator who checks every zone before we call it done. New automatic systems get a rain or freeze sensor. We check what permit your address requires and pull it before we dig. Already have a system that is not working? We fix heads, lines, valves and controllers too, on systems we did not install. Before a hard freeze, make sure the sensor works or the system is shut off.

faq.q: Do you install sprinkler systems in Big Sandy?
faq.a: Yes. We install and repair sprinkler systems in Big Sandy and out toward Hawkins, under a Texas licensed irrigator, and pull the permit the job requires. Pricing comes after a free walkthrough, and you get a written, itemized quote, usually within a day.

faq.q: How much does a sprinkler system cost?
faq.a: It depends on how much of the yard you want watered, how many zones that takes, whether the beds need drip and what your water source and pressure look like. We price irrigation after a free walkthrough instead of guessing from a phone call.

faq.q: Should my flower beds be on drip or spray?
faq.a: Drip, almost always. Spray heads in a bed wet the leaves, the mulch and the house and waste water to wind and evaporation. Drip puts water at the roots and keeps foliage dry, which helps against fungus in our humid springs. It also suits sandy ground, where water moves through quickly.

faq.q: Do you repair sprinkler systems you did not install?
faq.a: Yes. We fix broken heads and lines, leaking valves, zones that will not come on, bad wiring and controllers nobody has set since the house was built, on systems we put in and systems we did not. Send a quote request and we will walk the yard, find what is failing and quote the repair in writing.

faq.q: Do I need a permit for a sprinkler system?
faq.a: Many East Texas cities require one for a new irrigation system, and the rules vary by city. We check what your address requires and pull the permit before we start. We confirm the rules for your exact address on the walkthrough, then handle the paperwork so you do not have to.

If you want to see the layout first, the Landscape Design Preview is $199 for flower beds, $449 for hardscape and $999 for the full property.

Sandy soil and open sun shape the plant list. Sand takes water fast and gives it up fast, so we work compost into the beds and pick plants that take heat. Where the soil sits over clay, near the creek or a low corner, we adjust the grade so plants are not left standing in water. Rock beds get fabric underneath. Mulch beds do not. Plants are chosen for that exact spot, not for whatever was on sale that week.

Fall is the best planting window, September to about Thanksgiving, when the soil stays warm while the air cools and roots keep growing through the mild winter. The same crew handles the job from first shovel to last rake, and we haul off the debris before we leave. Walls, sod or drainage can be added to the same project if the plan needs them. We also walk you through watering the new plants through their first season.

faq.q: How much does landscaping cost in Big Sandy?
faq.a: Most landscaping and planting projects run $900 to $3,600. A small bed refresh starts at a few hundred dollars, and large custom designs run more. The size of the area, the plants and materials and how easy the site is to reach set the number. We walk it for free and send a written, itemized estimate.

faq.q: Can you make a country house look finished without a lot of upkeep?
faq.a: Yes. We keep beds close to the house, use shrubs that hold their shape, add a couple of trees for shade and scale and cut clean edges so mowing stays simple. Fewer, bigger beds are easier to keep up than lots of small ones.

faq.q: When is the best time to plant shrubs and trees here?
faq.a: Fall. From September through November the soil is warm while the air cools, so roots keep growing through winter. A shrub planted in October gets months of root growth before summer, while one planted in April gets about eight weeks before the first 100-degree day. Keep watering through winter.

faq.q: Do you put landscape fabric under mulch?
faq.a: No. Mulch breaks down into soil, and on top of fabric that soil becomes a seed bed. In two or three years weeds root through the sheet. We edge clean and mulch at 1 to 1.5 inches instead. Fabric does belong under river rock and gravel, and we install it there.

faq.q: Can I see the design before you build?
faq.a: Yes. The Landscape Design Preview shows renderings of the space with a plant list and bed layout before anything goes in the ground. It is $199 for flower beds, $449 for hardscape and $999 for the full property, with one round of revisions, credited toward an install booked within 90 days.

lawn-maintenance.h1: Weekly mowing for Big Sandy lots and acreage
lawn-maintenance.lede: Mowing, trimming and edging for Big Sandy yards with long fence lines and outbuildings, with the deck set for the grass you actually have and the same crew every visit.
lawn-maintenance.answer: Yard Dog Landscapes mows yards in Big Sandy from our base in Longview, about 25 miles east on US 80. We are family-owned, fully insured and rated 5.0 on Google across {{REVIEWS}} reviews.
lawn-maintenance.local_h: What mowing costs on a big, open Big Sandy lot
local: Open turf is the cheap part of a Big Sandy yard. The hours go into everything around it: fence lines, a barn or shop, a long drive, trees standing in the grass. Two properties with the same acreage can take very different amounts of time, so we walk the lot before we name a price. You get a flat per-visit number in writing. Typical yards start at $65 a visit, and bigger ground is priced to what we actually mow and trim.

You do not have to mow the whole place. Plenty of owners out here keep the ground around the house, the drive and the near fence lines sharp and let the back acreage stay natural. We price only the part we cut. Tell us where you want the line, and we will walk it with you so the same area gets the same treatment every week, no matter who in the family is home.

Most lots here run Bermuda in the open sun and St. Augustine only where the pines and hardwoods throw real shade. We set the deck for each one. Bermuda runs lower in spring and goes up to about two to two and a half inches for summer. St. Augustine stays at three and a half to four. Sand burns out fast in a dry August, and a taller cut shades the soil and slows that down.

Sand drains quickly on the high ground, but the low spots near Big Sandy Creek sit on clay and can stay soft after a storm. A wet corner is a drainage question, not a mowing one, and we will tell you if we see it. Big Sandy is an easy run west on US 80 past Gladewater, so weekly mowing works here. If you are out toward Hawkins or up toward Gilmer, send the address and we will confirm.

faq.q: How much does weekly mowing cost in Big Sandy?
faq.a: A typical yard starts at $65 per visit for weekly mowing. On an acre or more, the price depends on how much is open turf versus fence line, outbuildings and trim work. Heavy tree cover and gate access matter too. You get a flat per-visit price in writing before the first mow.

faq.q: Can you mow just the area around my house on a big lot?
faq.a: Yes. We can keep the lawn around the house, the drive and the nearby fence lines sharp and leave the outer ground alone. We price only the area we mow and trim, in writing, after a walkthrough. If you later want more of the lot cut, we adjust the price to match.

faq.q: What height will you cut Bermuda and St. Augustine?
faq.a: Bermuda runs about one to one and a half inches in spring and two to two and a half in summer. St. Augustine stays at three and a half to four inches all summer and never drops under three. If your yard has sunny Bermuda and a shaded St. Augustine section, we cut each at its own height.

faq.q: Do you bag the clippings?
faq.a: No. Clippings get blown back into the turf, where they hand a little nitrogen and moisture back to the soil. Early fall leaves are mulched back into the lawn with the mower. If the tree line drops more than the mower can handle, a full leaf cleanup is a separate service we can quote.

faq.q: Do you mow out toward Hawkins and up toward Gilmer?
faq.a: We work in Big Sandy and the country around it. Send your address with a quote request and we will confirm it is in range and set up a free walkthrough. Once we have walked the property, the written price tells you exactly what each weekly visit covers.

leaf-removal.title: Leaf Removal in Big Sandy, TX: Vacuum Trailer | Yard Dog
leaf-removal.meta: Leaf removal in Big Sandy, TX with the area's only leaf vacuum trailer. No bags, leaves shredded about 10 to 1, one flat price quoted after a free walkthrough.
leaf-removal.h1: Leaf cleanup for tree-lined Big Sandy lots
leaf-removal.lede: The tree line drops leaves and needles on your lawn edges every fall, and the wind spreads them across the open yard. We blow them out, vacuum them up and haul them off.
leaf-removal.answer: Yard Dog Landscapes is a family-owned, fully insured crew based in Longview, and we clear leaves in Big Sandy with the only leaf vacuum trailer in the area. We blow leaves and pine straw onto a paved surface, vacuum them up, shred them about 10 to 1 and haul them off, with no bags. It is one flat price, quoted after a free walkthrough. We are rated 5.0 on Google across {{REVIEWS}} reviews.
leaf-removal.local_h: Clearing leaves on a wooded Big Sandy lot
local: Pines and hardwoods ring a lot of Big Sandy properties, and every fall they drop needles and leaves along the edges. Then the wind carries it all across the open middle of the yard and into the foundation beds. A rake never catches up with that. The crew blows everything out of the lawn, the shrub beds and the rock beds onto a paved surface, and the vacuum trailer takes it from there.

A vacuum trailer needs somewhere to pull up, and country lots usually have room. On the walkthrough we look at where the trailer can reach, how far the piles sit from it and how long the hose run is. The hose reaches back into the yard for piles the trailer cannot get close to. That planning is built into the flat price, so a long drive does not turn into a surprise charge.

The volume out here is the real problem. Our vacuum shreds leaves about 10 to 1, so ten yards of leaves leave your place as one. Nothing is bagged, and nothing is mulched into the grass, where a heavy drop mats down and smothers it. We also re-edge any bed line the leaves buried, so the beds look cut again when we pull out. You get the yard back without a stack of bags to haul to the road.

Sweetgums let go in the first half of November, and post oaks and water oaks hang on and drop into February. On a lot with a heavy tree line, plan on mid-November, mid-December and one last pass before spring green-up. Before November the light drop is better mulched in with the mower. If you have St. Augustine near the trees, do not let a wet leaf mat sit on it.

faq.q: How much does leaf removal cost in Big Sandy?
faq.a: Leaf removal is one flat price for the job, quoted in writing before we start. There are no bag fees and no hourly meter. The price follows lot size, how many trees you have, how deep the leaves have piled and how many beds need clearing. Send a quote request and we will set up the walkthrough.

faq.q: Do you clear leaves out of beds and fence lines too?
faq.a: Yes. A full cleanup covers the lawn, beds, walks, drive and fence lines, and we haul the leaves off. On wooded lots the tree line keeps dropping into December, so a second pass is often worth scheduling. Bed lines the leaves buried get re-edged before we leave.

faq.q: Why a vacuum trailer instead of bags?
faq.a: Bags mean time spent filling them and a pile at the curb. The vacuum shreds leaves about 10 to 1, so one trailer hauls what would fill dozens of bags. We are the only crew in the area running one. You pay one flat price, not for bags or for the hours it takes to fill them.

faq.q: Can I keep the pine straw in my beds?
faq.a: Yes. Pine straw makes good mulch, so if you want it left in the beds, we leave it there and clear it off the lawn only. Tell us on the walkthrough which beds you want kept, and the written price will say so. Everything else on the property gets blown out and vacuumed.

faq.q: When should I book leaf removal near Big Sandy?
faq.a: Removal starts in the first half of November, when the sweetgums let go and the volume jumps in a few days. Post oaks and water oaks keep dropping into February, so a mid-December pass and a late-winter pass are common on lots with a heavy tree line. Booking early gets you the date you want.

mulch-installation.title: Mulch Installation in Big Sandy, TX | Yard Dog Landscapes
mulch-installation.meta: Mulch and bed refreshes in Big Sandy, TX: edges re-cut, weeds pulled, hardwood laid 1 to 1.5 inches deep. Most beds run $600 to $2,400.
mulch-installation.h1: Mulch and bed refreshes for Big Sandy homes
mulch-installation.lede: Clean edges, weeds pulled by the root and hardwood laid at the depth that works here, with rock kept where rock belongs.
mulch-installation.answer: Yard Dog Landscapes is a family-owned, fully insured crew based in Longview, and we mulch beds in Big Sandy. We re-cut the edges, pull weeds by the root, loosen the soil and lay hardwood, cypress, cedar, dyed mulch or pine straw 1 to 1.5 inches deep. Most beds run $600 to $2,400. We are rated 5.0 on Google across {{REVIEWS}} reviews.
mulch-installation.local_h: Rock along the foundation, mulch everywhere else
local: A lot of country homes around Big Sandy run rock along the foundation and mulch in the planted beds, and that split makes sense. Rock sheds roof water and stays put. Mulch feeds the plants. The one rule is the fabric: it goes under rock and gravel, and it never goes under mulch. We build each bed the way its material needs. We match the material that is already in a bed so it breaks down evenly.

Sand is why we like hardwood here. It breaks down over a season or two and feeds the sandy soil underneath, which has little organic matter of its own, and the layer slows evaporation between rains. We lay it 1 to 1.5 inches deep over a clean, edged bed, tapered off at stems and trunks. Three inches is a northern habit. Mulch is also kept off stems and trunks, so nothing sits wet against the bark.

Pricing follows the beds. We measure the square footage, and for fresh mulch you divide it by 260 to get yards, so a 1,000 square foot run of beds takes about 4 yards. On bigger jobs we bring bulk mulch by the yard, so you pay for mulch and not bags. Most beds run $600 to $2,400, and a thin top-dress costs less. We measure first, so you only pay for what the beds need.

Windows are late April through mid-May, and late September through October. The fall top-dress goes down before the tree line drops its leaves, which keeps beds looking finished into winter. Do not scrape the old layer off first, because it is turning into soil. If leaves bury the beds before you get to it, a leaf cleanup clears them first. We pull weeds first, since mulch hides weeds and does not kill them.

faq.q: How much does mulch installation cost in Big Sandy?
faq.a: Most mulch and bed refreshes run $600 to $2,400. The number depends on how many beds you have, how many yards of mulch they take, the type and how much edging and weed pulling they need. A fall top-dress over a layer that is still there costs less than a full install.

faq.q: Should I use rock or mulch in my beds?
faq.a: Rock works along foundations and in drainage channels, and it gets fabric under it. Mulch is better in planted beds, because it breaks down and feeds the soil, and it should never have fabric under it. We lay hardwood 1 to 1.5 inches deep over a clean, edged bed.

faq.q: How deep should mulch be?
faq.a: About 1 to 1.5 inches over a prepped bed. Three inches sheds light rain, holds moisture against stems until they rot and gives voles cover through the winter. For a 2,000 square foot bed that is about 8 yards, not the 19 an online calculator will tell you to buy.

faq.q: What kind of mulch do you use?
faq.a: Shredded hardwood is the standard for most beds. Cypress breaks down slower, cedar holds up well in our heat and humidity, and dyed black or brown gives more contrast. Pine straw is available if you like the look. On a refresh we match what is already in the bed.

faq.q: How often should mulch be refreshed?
faq.a: Most beds need a thin layer once a year, usually in spring. In fall, push a finger down through the mulch until you hit soil. If an inch is left, add an inch. That older layer is turning into soil and feeding shallow-rooted shrubs, so leave it in place.

retaining-walls.title: Retaining Walls in Big Sandy, TX | Yard Dog Landscapes
retaining-walls.meta: Retaining walls in Big Sandy, TX for lots that drop to a creek or ditch: compacted base, gravel backfill and a drain behind every wall. Most run $3,000 to $19,000.
retaining-walls.h1: Retaining walls for sloped Big Sandy lots
retaining-walls.lede: Where a lot drops to a creek or a ditch and the soil washes with every heavy rain, a wall holds the grade and gives you flat ground to use.
retaining-walls.answer: Yard Dog Landscapes is a family-owned, fully insured crew based in Longview, and we build retaining walls in Big Sandy. We build segmental block, natural stone, boulder and timber walls on a compacted base with gravel backfill and a drain behind them. Height and length set the price. Most walls run $3,000 to $19,000, and tall structural walls run $20,000 and up. We are rated 5.0 on Google across {{REVIEWS}} reviews.
retaining-walls.local_h: Holding the grade where a Big Sandy lot drops away
local: Some Big Sandy lots drop off toward Big Sandy Creek or a ditch. On those slopes, soil can wash out with every heavy rain, and the bank loses ground a little at a time. A low wall holds the grade and turns the slope into a flat bed or a patio pad. We walk the slope first, measure the grade change and trace where the water comes from. A short wall can also set up a level spot for a bed or a bench.

Sand makes the foundation of the wall the first thing we check. Loose sand will not hold block set on undisturbed ground, so we dig below grade, compact a crushed stone base and set the first course dead level. Every course above inherits that bottom row. Skip this step and a wall can lean within a few seasons. A real base and a level first course are most of what keeps a wall straight for years, and they are the part nobody sees once it is backfilled.

Water is the second thing. Rain runs down the slope and soaks in behind the wall, and in the clay pockets it has nowhere to go. We build a gravel chimney and a perforated drain behind every wall, tied out to daylight or a pop-up emitter. Taller walls also get geogrid tied back into the hill. A wall over about four feet usually needs an engineered plan, and we tell you at the walkthrough.

Height and length move the price most. A short garden wall starts at a few thousand dollars, most walls run $3,000 to $19,000 and tall structural walls pass $20,000. Block, natural stone, boulders and pressure-treated timber all work, and the choice depends on the look and the load. A wall that is already leaning gets taken down and rebuilt right. We price each wall after walking the slope and send it in writing, itemized.

faq.q: What does a small retaining wall cost in Big Sandy?
faq.a: Short garden walls start at a few thousand dollars. Most walls run $3,000 to $19,000 depending on height and length, and tall structural walls can pass $20,000. We price each one after walking the slope, because the base and the drainage behind the wall are a big part of the work.

faq.q: Do retaining walls need drainage?
faq.a: Yes, and it is the most important part of the build. Water that collects behind a wall builds pressure and pushes it out over time. Every wall we build gets gravel backfill and a perforated drain that carries water to daylight or a pop-up emitter, so pressure never builds.

faq.q: How tall can you build a wall?
faq.a: We build everything from short garden and seating walls to tall structural walls. Walls over about four feet usually need engineered design and reinforcement such as geogrid. If your wall calls for a stamped engineering plan, we will tell you during the walkthrough.

faq.q: Which material is best for a wall near a creek or ditch?
faq.a: For most yards, segmental block, which locks together and flexes with the ground. Natural stone and boulder walls cost more and look great on the right property. Pressure-treated timber fits some jobs. We pick based on the slope, the water and the look, and put it in the estimate.

faq.q: Can a leaning wall be fixed?
faq.a: Propping it up will not hold. A leaning wall almost always has a base or drainage problem, and the real fix is taking it down and rebuilding it on a compacted base with drainage behind it. We will tell you at the walkthrough what yours needs.

sod-installation.title: Sod Installation in Big Sandy, TX | Yard Dog Landscapes
sod-installation.meta: Sod installation in Big Sandy, TX: Bermuda in open sun, St. Augustine in real shade, laid on prepped ground. Most projects run $1,500 to $4,700 by the pallet.
sod-installation.h1: New sod for the front and around the house in Big Sandy
sod-installation.lede: Strip, level, amend and lay, with the right grass for the sun you really get and a watering plan that fits sandy ground.
sod-installation.answer: Yard Dog Landscapes is a family-owned, fully insured crew based in Longview, and we lay sod in Big Sandy. We strip old turf, level and amend the soil, then lay Bermuda, St. Augustine or Zoysia with tight, staggered seams and starter fertilizer. Most projects run $1,500 to $4,700, priced by the pallet. We are rated 5.0 on Google across {{REVIEWS}} reviews.
sod-installation.local_h: Sodding the part of a big lot that shows
local: On a large Big Sandy lot, sodding the whole thing is rarely the right move. We usually recommend the front and the area around the house, where lawn shows and gets used, and leaving the outer ground as it is. That keeps you inside the $1,500 to $4,700 range most projects land in. Sod is priced by the pallet, so we measure the square footage on site and quote from that.

Sun picks the grass. Lots here have open sun in the middle and tree lines around the edges. Bermuda, usually Tif419, wants six to eight hours of direct sun, so it goes in the open ground. St. Augustine, in Floratam, Palmetto or Raleigh depending on the shade, goes only where the shade is real. Under about four hours of sun no turf lasts, and that spot is better as a bed.

Prep matters more on sand. We strip the old turf and weeds to bare dirt, regrade where water needs to move, and till in two to three inches of compost or topsoil so the ground can hold water. Then we level and roll it. If a low corner near the creek stays wet, we fix the grade or the drainage before any sod goes down on it. Prep is the difference between sod that holds for years and sod that thins out by year two.

Timing and water finish the job. Bermuda goes down best from late April through August, and St. Augustine from May through September, finishing by the end of September. Sandy ground dries quickly, so the first two weeks of deep morning watering decide whether the sod takes. We leave you a written schedule, and we avoid laying in a stretch when you cannot water every day. Evening watering keeps the blades wet overnight and invites fungus, so mornings it is.

faq.q: How much does sod installation cost in Big Sandy?
faq.a: Most projects run $1,500 to $4,700, priced by the pallet. Small patch repairs cost less, and full front-yard installs with heavy prep cost more. Removing old turf, grading and soil amendment add to the total. We measure on site and send a written quote.

faq.q: Do I have to sod my whole lot?
faq.a: No, and on acreage we usually say don't. Sodding the front and the area around the house covers what shows and gets used. We map the sun and the layout on the walkthrough and tell you where sod makes sense and where the existing ground can stay.

faq.q: When is the best time to lay sod in Big Sandy?
faq.a: Bermuda goes down best from late April through August, and St. Augustine from May through September, when the ground is warm. St. Augustine needs four to six weeks of root growth before dormancy, so get it in by the end of September.

faq.q: How often should I water new sod?
faq.a: Every morning for the first two weeks or so, deep enough to soak through into the soil below, until the roots grab. Then taper to two deep waterings a week that finish around sunrise. Evening watering keeps the blades wet all night, which invites fungus. We leave you a written schedule.

faq.q: Can you fix bare or dead patches?
faq.a: Yes. We repair patches with sod or plugs as well as laying full yards. St. Augustine spreads only by surface runners, so a dead spot bigger than a few feet across will not close on its own before weeds find the bare dirt. Late summer is still a fine time to patch.

tree-planting.title: Tree Planting in Big Sandy, TX | Yard Dog Landscapes
tree-planting.meta: Tree planting in Big Sandy, TX: oaks and magnolias for drained ground, bald cypress for wet spots, planted at the root flare. Quoted after a free walkthrough.
tree-planting.h1: Shade trees for open Big Sandy lots
tree-planting.lede: Real shade trees for lots with room to grow, matched to the high sand or the wet low corner, set at the right depth and followed by a watering plan.
tree-planting.answer: Yard Dog Landscapes is a family-owned, fully insured crew based in Longview, and we plant trees in Big Sandy. We help you pick a species for your ground and sun, plant it with the root flare at grade, build a watering basin and mulch ring and leave a written watering plan. Cost depends on species, size, number and access, so we quote after a free walkthrough. We are rated 5.0 on Google across {{REVIEWS}} reviews.
tree-planting.local_h: Picking the right tree for the right corner of the lot
local: The big lots around Big Sandy have something many town yards do not: room. A tree planted here can reach its full size without crowding a roof or a power line. That makes mature size the first question. A Natchez crepe myrtle wants 25 to 30 feet, an Acoma stays near 10, and an oak keeps going. We read the spot and the space before we recommend anything. Stock comes from regional growers, and we would usually rather plant a smaller tree that roots in fast.

Ground decides the species. Oaks and southern magnolias want soil that drains, which fits the sandy high ground. Down in a wet pocket near the creek or a ditch, where water sits after a rain, bald cypress and river birch handle wet feet far better. We check how long water stays on a spot before we choose a tree for it. If a spot is too wet even for those, we will say so and suggest moving the tree to higher ground.

Sand creates its own problem for a new tree. A container tree comes in a ball of light potting mix, and in sandy ground the water around it drains away quickly, so the ball can dry out fast in summer. That is why the watering plan matters as much as the planting. We soak the ball itself, and you get the schedule in writing. Skipping the soak is how spring trees die in August in yards that got watered.

We plant year-round, but fall is the best window, from September until around Thanksgiving, and the cold months work well for dormant stock. We dig a wide, shallow hole, set the root flare at grade, cut circling roots, put native soil back and lay a mulch ring off the trunk. We stake only on a windy, exposed site, and an open lot can be one. Wide holes suit roots here, because they run sideways rather than deep.

faq.q: How much does tree planting cost in Big Sandy?
faq.a: We quote after a walkthrough instead of publishing a price, because the tree itself drives most of the cost. Species, size at planting, how many trees and how easy the spot is to reach all matter. You get a written quote with the tree, the planting and the aftercare plan spelled out.

faq.q: What trees grow in a wet spot near the creek?
faq.a: Bald cypress and river birch both handle wet feet better than most trees. Oaks and magnolias want ground that drains. We check how long water sits after a rain before we pick a tree for a low spot, and we will tell you if a spot is too wet for what you had in mind.

faq.q: When is the best time to plant a tree here?
faq.a: Fall, from September until around Thanksgiving. The soil stays warm after the air cools, so the tree gets months of root growth before summer. Spring planting works, but it needs more watering through the first summer, and dry sandy ground makes that more important.

faq.q: How do I water a new tree on sandy ground?
faq.a: Soak the root ball itself with a hose on a trickle for about twenty minutes. For a fall tree, do that twice a week for six weeks, weekly through November, then every ten to fourteen days in a dry winter. Soak everything new the day before a hard freeze. We leave this in writing.

faq.q: Should I buy the biggest tree I can afford?
faq.a: Usually not. A seven-gallon tree planted in October typically catches up to a thirty-gallon tree planted the same day within about four years, because it roots in faster and skips a summer in shock. Bigger trees cost more and need more water. We size the tree to the spot.

tree-shrub-care.title: Tree & Shrub Care in Big Sandy, TX | Yard Dog Landscapes
tree-shrub-care.meta: Tree and shrub pruning in Big Sandy, TX: dead limbs, crepe myrtle thinning, overgrown shrubs and small tree removal, quoted after a free walkthrough.
tree-shrub-care.h1: Pruning and shrub care for wooded Big Sandy lots
tree-shrub-care.lede: Dead lower limbs, crepe myrtles that need thinning, shrubs that have crept over the walk and small trees that have outgrown their spot, handled and hauled off.
tree-shrub-care.answer: Yard Dog Landscapes is a family-owned, fully insured crew based in Longview, and we prune trees and shrubs in Big Sandy. We thin crepe myrtles instead of topping them, clear dead lower limbs, remove small trees and shrubs and haul off every cut. Price depends on how many plants, their size and condition, so we quote in writing after a free walkthrough. We are rated 5.0 on Google across {{REVIEWS}} reviews.
tree-shrub-care.local_h: Working the trees and shrubs near a Big Sandy house
local: On a wooded Big Sandy lot, the trees that matter most are the ones near the house and the drive. We start there. Dead lower limbs on shade trees shade the lawn and get in the way of the mower, so we take those off with clean cuts at the branch collar. We walk the property, flag what needs work and what should be left alone, and put it in a written quote.

Shrubs near the house are the other half of the job. After a few seasons on open, sunny ground, they crowd the walks, press on the siding and grow into the beds. We prune each one in its own window: azaleas right after bloom, hollies and boxwoods in early summer, crepe myrtles and knockout roses in February. Dead wood comes out whenever we see it. Cuts are sized to what the plant can close, and every limb and trimming gets raked up and hauled off.

Crepe myrtles are common in country yards, and a lot of them have been topped. We do not top them. We thin them, take out crossing and rubbing branches and limb them up so the bark shows. A topped tree can take two or three winters to recover, so we plan it out and come back each dormant season. Oaks are left alone in spring and early summer because of oak wilt.

Some jobs belong to someone else, and we say so. We remove small trees and overgrown shrubs and clear storm limbs, but we do not take down large trees near a house or grind stumps. That is work for a tree service with the right equipment. A pine or hardwood leaning over the roof gets flagged on the walkthrough, not guessed at. We would rather tell you that up front than start a job we should not.

faq.q: How much does tree and shrub care cost in Big Sandy?
faq.a: We quote after a free walkthrough rather than publishing a price, because it swings with how many plants you have, their size and condition and what each one needs. Light shaping on a few shrubs is a different job from recovering a row of topped crepe myrtles. You get a written, itemized quote.

faq.q: Can you clear small trees and overgrown shrubs around the house?
faq.a: Yes. We remove small trees and overgrown shrubs that have outgrown their spot, prune what stays and haul off the debris. Big trees, especially near the house, are a job for a tree service, and we will tell you when that is the case.

faq.q: When should crepe myrtles be pruned?
faq.a: February, while the tree is dormant and before the buds break. Take out suckers, crossing branches and dead twigs, and keep the cuts up top to pencil thickness. Do not top the trunks back to knuckles. A crepe myrtle blooms on new wood on its own, so a hard cut does not make it flower more.

faq.q: When is it safe to prune an oak?
faq.a: Not in spring or early summer. Oak wilt spreads partly through beetles drawn to fresh pruning cuts, and they are most active then. We prune oaks in the dead of winter or the heat of late summer. A storm-broken oak limb is cut clean and sealed right away.

faq.q: Do you clean up storm limbs?
faq.a: Yes. We clear downed limbs and storm debris from the yard, trim the broken ends back to clean cuts and haul everything off. If the damage is a big tree on or leaning against the house, that is a tree service job, and we will say so at the walkthrough.
